channel.title: The Epoch Institute — Research Series
channel.description: Thematic essays on civilisational rise and collapse.

item.title: Series 14 — Christmas Day in History
item.description: Crownings, Truces and Crossings on 25 December. From Aurelian's temple to the Sun in 274 to Gorbachev's resignation in 1991: how a midwinter feast became a day for crowning kings, for crossing rivers by night, for laying down arms, and for carols and stories.

item.title: Series 13 — Midwinter
item.description: How the World Has Marked the Darkest Days. From Saturnalia and Yule to Dongzhi, Yalda Night and Inti Raymi: how societies have marked the winter solstice and the weeks around it, and how their feasts, gift-bringers and songs borrowed from, replaced and outlived one another.

item.title: Series 12 — The Written Word
item.description: How Thirty-Two Languages Were Written, Carried, Outlived Their States and Came Back. From the accounts of Uruk to the schools that brought back Hebrew and Hawaiian: how thirty-two languages were first written, carried by empires and faiths, outlived their states and were read again.

item.title: Series 11 — From Ruler to Enslaved
item.description: What Fifty Social Ladders Show Side by Side. From Hammurabi's Babylonia to Saint-Domingue and Stalin's Soviet Union: how fifty societies ranked their people, who was owned or bound, how people rose and fell, and how uncertain the numbers are.

item.title: Series 10 — Who Invented It First?
item.description: Firsts, Credit and the Long Road of Ideas. From stone tools 3.3 million years ago to the World Wide Web: what 291 inventions and discoveries show about firsts made more than once, credit given and withheld, named inventors and anonymous makers, and why "first" is so often disputed.

item.title: Series 09 — Faiths on the Move
item.description: How Thirty Religions Spread, Met and Ended. From the city gods of Sumer to the Bahá'í Faith: how thirty religions began, were carried by kings, merchants, missionaries, soldiers and the enslaved, met and borrowed from one another, and came in some places to their last temple.

item.title: Series 08 — How Songs Travel
item.description: The Evolution, Branching and Power of Song. From the Lament for Ur to Glory to Hong Kong: how 300 songs kept through history passed from hymn to anthem, lent their tunes across borders, were put to work by states and parties, and outlived the powers that sang or banned them.

item.title: Series 07 — Before the State
item.description: How Peoples Lived Without Kings, and Some Still Do. From the Natufian villages of the Levant and the Jōmon potters of Japan to the Māori, Mapuche, Sámi, Ainu and Taíno of today: how peoples ordered their lives without a state, and what forty-five cultures show beside a register of 5,468 states.

item.title: Series 06 — Who Should Rule?
item.description: One, Few or Many: Forms of Government Compared. From Athenian assemblies and Venetian councils to absolute kings and juntas: how twenty forms of government answered Aristotle's questions of who should rule and for whose good, and what the record shows.

item.title: Series 05 — The Military Revolution
item.description: Technology, Tactics, and the Shifting Balance of Power. How advances in military technology — the stirrup, gunpowder, the warship — reshaped the competitive landscape between polities and enabled otherwise peripheral states to become world powers.

item.title: Series 04 — Cross-Cultural Exchange
item.description: How Empires Spread — and Were Changed by — Ideas and Culture. From Hellenisation to the Islamic Golden Age to the Columbian Exchange, this series explores the two-way nature of cultural contact under imperial conditions and its lasting consequences.

item.title: Series 03 — The Collapse Problem
item.description: Common Patterns in Imperial Decline Across Five Millennia. Why do empires fall? Comparing the trajectories of the Western Roman Empire, the Abbasid Caliphate, the Mongol Empire, and others to identify recurring structural vulnerabilities.

item.title: Series 02 — Trade and Territory
item.description: Economic Networks Across the Ancient and Medieval World. A study of how control over trade routes, currency systems, and agricultural surplus shaped imperial ambition, and how economic disruption so often proved fatal to imperial order.

item.title: Series 01 — The Architecture of Power
item.description: How Empires Build the Structures That Sustain Them. An examination of the administrative, legal, and infrastructural systems that allowed large-scale polities to persist, and why their absence almost always preceded collapse.
